paragraphs: Logical Credal Networks represent knowledge using logical statements whose probabilities can lie within bounds. They can express both marginal and conditional probability bounds and accommodate cycles. This makes them useful for reasoning when knowledge does not justify a single precise probability. Earlier work concentrated on calculating lower and upper posterior probabilities for a query.

This paper moves from evaluating queries to finding explanations for observed evidence. It formally defines MAP and Marginal MAP reasoning tasks within this framework. These tasks concern selecting likely explanations, with Marginal MAP also accounting for variables outside the explanation being selected. Establishing these definitions gives explanation seeking a precise meaning in a setting with imprecise probabilities.

The authors develop search methods that solve the tasks exactly, then introduce approximate alternatives intended to handle larger instances. An extensive evaluation covers randomly generated networks and networks drawn from more realistic use cases. The reported results support the effectiveness of these algorithms, extending Logical Credal Networks from probability estimation toward evidence based explanation.
neurips-2024-abductive-reasoning-in-logi.tldr: The paper defines and solves explanation-finding tasks in Logical Credal Networks, combining exact search with scalable approximations.

paragraphs: Monocular depth estimation predicts distances from a single color image. This paper investigates a weakness in models trained for autonomous driving: their estimates of obstacle depth can depend heavily on the surrounding road region. The authors observe this dependence across models with different architectures, suggesting that image context can influence depth predictions for multiple traffic participants.

Their Adversarial Road Marking attack places an optimized visual patch on the road and disguises it as an ordinary marking. Earlier patch attacks attached the pattern to a particular obstacle. Separating the patch from the obstacle changes the attack's reach: a road patch can affect depth predictions for participants other than an object carrying the patch, creating a continuing threat in that environment.

Experiments using dataset simulations and real-world scenarios report effectiveness, stealthiness, and robustness across various depth models. The reported Mean Relative Shift Ratio is about 1.507 over eight models. These findings identify road context as a consequential vulnerability in the evaluated systems and show why testing only patches attached to obstacles can miss a broader attack mechanism.
neurips-2024-beware-of-road-markings-a-n.tldr: Adversarial patches disguised as road markings exploit depth models' reliance on road context to affect predictions for traffic participants.

paragraphs: Language models can become overconfident when adapted to specialized tasks, especially when little training data is available. One response is to estimate uncertainty through an approximate Bayesian treatment after training. The paper argues that this timing creates a bottleneck: the uncertainty estimate remains constrained by parameters learned without that joint treatment during training.

Bayesian Low-Rank Adaptation by Backpropagation, or BLoB, brings uncertainty learning into the fine-tuning process itself. It continuously adjusts both the mean and covariance of model parameters. The mean describes their central values, while covariance describes uncertainty and how parameter variations relate to one another. Learning these together allows the adaptation process to account for both parameter estimates and their uncertainty.

The authors report empirical evidence that BLoB is effective for generalization and uncertainty estimation on both in-distribution and out-of-distribution data. These evaluations address whether the adapted model performs well and whether its uncertainty remains informative when the data changes. The contribution is a training-time approach to Bayesian adaptation, supported by results across both evaluation settings.
neurips-2024-blob-bayesian-low-rank-adap.tldr: BLoB jointly learns parameter values and uncertainty throughout language-model fine-tuning, with reported benefits for generalization and uncertainty estimation.

paragraphs: Test-time adaptation helps a pretrained vision-language model adjust to incoming data without advance knowledge of its target domain. Existing approaches face different tradeoffs. Methods that optimize entropy during testing can require substantial computation, while some methods that avoid training leave useful information within the current test example underused. BoostAdapter connects these two sources of adaptation.

The method maintains a lightweight key-value memory for retrieving features from two kinds of samples. Historical samples are filtered from the incoming test stream and capture information about the target distribution. Boosting samples come from regional bootstrapping and capture information specific to the current example. Combining them lets adaptation draw on both accumulated experience and the image being processed.

This distinction matters because understanding the broader test distribution and understanding a particular test instance provide complementary information. The authors give a theoretical justification for their approach and evaluate it on out-of-distribution and cross-domain datasets. The reported findings support the effectiveness of this combined memory mechanism and its applicability to varied deployment situations.
neurips-2024-boostadapter-improving-visi.tldr: BoostAdapter adapts vision-language models using a lightweight memory that combines historical test samples with regional information from the current sample.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks build node representations by combining information from surrounding nodes. With many layers, these representations can become difficult to distinguish, a problem called over-smoothing. This paper examines that process through overlapping neighborhood subgraphs: as information travels farther, the large neighborhoods contributing to different nodes can become increasingly similar.

The authors use this view to explain why residual methods can help. Combining information from several neighborhood orders preserves distinctions that may disappear when relying on a single large neighborhood. They also identify two shortcomings in previous residual approaches: insufficient adaptation to individual nodes and substantial loss of information from higher-order neighborhoods. These observations motivate their Posterior-Sampling-based, Node-Adaptive Residual module, PSNR.

PSNR is designed to address both shortcomings while alleviating over-smoothing. The paper provides theoretical support that the module can reduce these problems and reports extensive experiments on node classification with fully observed data and with missing features. The findings support preserving useful information from farther neighborhoods while adapting the residual mechanism to the node being represented.
neurips-2024-deep-graph-neural-networks-.tldr: PSNR uses node-adaptive residual connections to alleviate over-smoothing while retaining useful information from higher-order graph neighborhoods.

paragraphs: A language model's ability to recall a fact can depend on how its context is written. Experiments with open-source models show that changing the context can manipulate retrieval even when the factual meaning remains the same. This suggests that successful recall may depend partly on cues in the wording, beyond the information that the context explicitly conveys.

The authors investigate an associative-memory interpretation of this behavior. Under that interpretation, particular tokens serve as clues that bring stored information into use. To study a concrete mechanism, they formulate a simple latent concept association problem and analyze a one-layer transformer. This controlled setting connects the observed sensitivity to context with a mathematical account of information retrieval.

Their theoretical and empirical results assign complementary roles to two transformer components: self-attention gathers relevant information, and the value matrix serves an associative-memory function. This establishes a mechanism in the studied setting and supports the broader possibility that language models behave like associative memories. It does not turn that interpretation into a universal account of factual recall.
neurips-2024-do-llms-dream-of-elephants-.tldr: Context-sensitive fact recall motivates an associative-memory account, which the authors analyze theoretically and empirically in a one-layer transformer.

paragraphs: Multimodal prediction becomes difficult when the available inputs vary from case to case. Some modalities may be missing, and observations may arrive sparsely or at irregular times. Limited access to high-quality training samples compounds these problems. FuseMoE addresses this combination of challenges through a framework designed to integrate diverse modalities under imperfect data collection conditions.

The framework uses a mixture of experts within a transformer architecture, together with a new gating function. The gate governs how the experts contribute to processing the available information. Its role is central to the paper: the authors connect their gating design theoretically to improved convergence rates, making it part of the learning argument as well as the architecture.

FuseMoE is designed to work with missing modalities and irregularly sampled trajectories, so its fusion mechanism accommodates variation in what is observed and when. Evaluations on a diverse set of challenging prediction tasks support its practical utility. The contribution combines flexibility in handling incomplete multimodal inputs with theoretical and empirical support for the proposed learning mechanism.
neurips-2024-fusemoe-mixture-of-experts-.tldr: FuseMoE combines expert models through a new gate to handle diverse, missing, and irregularly sampled modalities.

paragraphs: Many 3D generative adversarial networks rely on costly volume rendering based on casting rays through a scene. Gaussian splatting offers an explicit 3D representation with faster rasterization-based rendering. However, the authors find that a naive Gaussian generator can train unstably and produce visual artifacts because Gaussian positions and scales lack suitable guidance.

GSGAN addresses this problem with a hierarchy of Gaussians at multiple scales. Finer Gaussians are defined relative to coarser ones: their positions stay near their coarser counterparts, and their scales decrease as the hierarchy becomes finer. This arrangement gives the generator a structured way to represent broad scene content and small details while regulating where its components appear and how large they become.

The reported experiments show roughly 100-fold faster rendering than state-of-the-art 3D-consistent GANs, with comparable 3D generation capability. The result ties rendering efficiency to an architectural change that makes Gaussian representations workable in adversarial generation. Its significance is the combination of an efficient representation and a hierarchy that addresses the observed instability of a straightforward implementation.
neurips-2024-gsgan-adversarial-learning-.tldr: GSGAN organizes generated Gaussians into a controlled hierarchy, reporting 100-fold faster rendering with comparable 3D generation capability.

paragraphs: Point cloud recognition models can perform well on standard benchmarks while remaining vulnerable to corrupted inputs. Most augmentation methods address this in spatial coordinates. The paper instead studies frequency structure, motivated by the difficulty of understanding corruption in point clouds with sparse information and substantial spatial redundancy. A graph Fourier transform provides the basis for this analysis.

The authors observe a correlation between corruption robustness and model sensitivity to different frequency bands. They measure this sensitivity using the graph Fourier spectrum of the model's Jacobian, which describes how model outputs respond to input changes. This connects robustness to the kinds of frequency variation that particularly affect a model's predictions.

Their Frequency Adversarial Training method uses adversarial examples constructed in the frequency domain as training augmentation. The goal is to reduce sensitivity and improve resistance to corruptions. The paper supplies a theoretical guarantee concerning out-of-distribution generalization and reports extensive experiments across several architectures, achieving new state-of-the-art results. The findings support frequency-domain analysis as a useful guide for designing robustness training.
neurips-2024-improving-robustness-of-3d-.tldr: Frequency Adversarial Training uses graph Fourier analysis to target sensitivities associated with corruption vulnerability in point cloud recognition.

paragraphs: Training natural-sounding speech synthesis requires substantial high-quality audio, which is scarce for many Indian languages. This work repurposes conversational recordings originally collected for speech recognition in lower-quality environments. Its pipeline applies denoising and speech enhancement models trained on English to Indian languages, using their ability to generalize across languages to improve the recordings.

The resulting IndicVoices-R dataset contains 1,704 hours of speech from 10,496 speakers across 22 Indian languages. The authors report quality matching established speech synthesis datasets. They also introduce a benchmark for evaluating how synthesis models generalize to speakers under zero-shot, few-shot, and many-shot conditions, with diversity in age, gender, and speaking style.

Fine-tuning an English-pretrained model on both IndicTTS and IndicVoices-R improves zero-shot speaker generalization compared with using IndicTTS alone. The evaluation also finds limited zero-shot generalization to Indian voices in models trained on earlier datasets. These results support expanding speaker and language-family diversity through restored recognition data, alongside releasing the dataset and code for all 22 official Indian languages.
neurips-2024-indicvoices-r-unlocking-a-m.tldr: IndicVoices-R restores conversational speech into a large Indian-language synthesis dataset and improves zero-shot speaker generalization in the reported fine-tuning comparison.

paragraphs: Latent Bayesian optimization searches a continuous representation space to solve problems whose original inputs are high-dimensional or discrete. An encoder-decoder connects that space to candidate solutions, while a surrogate predicts their objective values. The authors identify a misalignment problem: reconstruction errors can break the correspondence between a latent representation and the candidate whose objective was evaluated.

InvBO is a plug-in module with two components. Its inversion method searches for a latent code that reconstructs the given target data completely, addressing the mismatch at its source. Its second component changes how a local search region is positioned. Instead of choosing its center solely from an existing objective value, it also considers the region's potential to support further optimization.

These components target complementary obstacles: inaccurate training relationships for the surrogate and unpromising choices about where to search next. Experiments on nine real-world benchmarks, including molecule design and arithmetic expression fitting, demonstrate the module's effectiveness. The findings support improving both the correspondence between latent codes and candidates and the selection of local search regions.
neurips-2024-inversion-based-latent-baye.tldr: InvBO improves latent Bayesian optimization by seeking reconstructing latent codes and choosing local search centers for their optimization potential.

paragraphs: World models let agents explore imagined outcomes to support decisions in the real world. Building them from video generators requires interactivity: the model must connect visual changes with an agent's actions and rewards. iVideoGPT addresses this by putting visual observations, actions, and rewards into a shared sequence of tokens processed by an autoregressive transformer.

Predicting subsequent tokens provides the framework for interactive modeling. A compressive tokenization method converts high-dimensional visual observations into discrete representations efficiently, helping make the approach scalable. The authors pretrain the model on millions of human and robotic manipulation trajectories, creating a foundation that can then be adapted for different downstream uses.

The evaluated applications include predicting video conditioned on actions, visual planning, and model-based reinforcement learning. iVideoGPT achieves performance competitive with state-of-the-art methods in these settings. The contribution is a common sequence-modeling framework that links video generation to agent interaction, supported by large-scale pretraining and results across multiple uses of learned world models.
neurips-2024-ivideogpt-interactive-video.tldr: iVideoGPT models observations, actions, and rewards as tokens, enabling scalable pretraining for interactive prediction, planning, and reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: This paper develops a faster algorithm for computing an approximate John ellipsoid around a collection of points in a high-dimensional space. The earlier approach repeatedly calculates leverage scores for the points and uses those scores to update their weights. These repeated calculations create an opportunity for improvement in the cost of the overall procedure.

The authors change when accurate scores are computed. Sampling allows the algorithm to postpone high-accuracy leverage-score calculations. Later, it processes multiple batches of accurate scores together using fast rectangular matrix multiplication. The central idea is to organize expensive work so that it can benefit from efficient batched computation, rather than performing every accurate update immediately.

The paper shows that this delayed-update strategy can substantially accelerate the existing approach. It also develops streaming algorithms that use little storage, drawing on similar ideas. Together, these contributions address both computation and memory demands for approximate John ellipsoids. The result highlights how changing the schedule and grouping of updates can improve an established iterative algorithm.
neurips-2024-john-ellipsoids-via-lazy-up.tldr: Delaying and batching accurate leverage-score calculations yields faster approximate John ellipsoid algorithms and low-space streaming variants.

paragraphs: Language models can translate human instructions into robot task plans, but long tasks become difficult when several robots must cooperate with incomplete knowledge of their environment. A plan must remain useful across many actions even as execution reveals new information. LLaMAR addresses this challenge with a language-model-based planning architecture for partially observable multi-agent settings.

Its framework cycles through planning, acting, correcting, and verifying. Feedback from executed actions supports self-correction, allowing the planner to revise its behavior as the task unfolds. The correction mechanism does not rely on oracles or simulators. This places action feedback at the center of maintaining a long-horizon plan under incomplete observation.

The authors also introduce MAP-THOR, a test suite containing household tasks of varying complexity within AI2-THOR. Experiments on MAP-THOR and Search & Rescue tasks report a 30% higher success rate than other state-of-the-art language-model-based multi-agent planners. These results support the value of explicitly organizing planning around execution feedback and verification for the evaluated long-horizon tasks.
neurips-2024-long-horizon-planning-for-m.tldr: LLaMAR uses a plan-act-correct-verify cycle to improve long-horizon multi-agent planning through feedback from executed actions.

paragraphs: A deployed classifier can change the data it will later encounter. Performative learning studies this feedback between a model's decisions and its environment. This paper represents the resulting distribution changes as push-forward measures: a shift operator transforms the underlying data distribution. The framework assumes knowledge of that operator without requiring a full specification of the data distribution.

This formulation encompasses existing models and supports new ways to estimate performative gradients, enabling more efficient and scalable learning strategies. It can also connect with models built around changes of variables, including variational autoencoders and normalizing flows. The shift operator provides a common mathematical object for describing how deployment changes the learning problem.

For classification with a performative effect linear in the parameters, the authors prove convexity under a new set of assumptions. Their condition restricts the direction of the effect rather than its strength, requiring classification to become harder as more accurate models are deployed. In this setting, they also derive a min-max connection to adversarially robust classification and illustrate the approach on synthetic and real data.
neurips-2024-optimal-classification-unde.tldr: Modeling deployment-induced shifts through transformation operators yields new learning methods and conditional convexity results for performative classification.

paragraphs: This paper treats electric circuits as a design language for convex optimization algorithms. The approach begins with an optimization problem and constructs a suitable circuit using ideas from resistor-inductor-capacitor systems. Its continuous-time behavior is designed to converge to a solution of that problem, connecting the circuit's dynamics with the mathematical objective.

The next step converts those continuous dynamics into updates that a computer can execute one step at a time. This discretization is automated and computer assisted, and the resulting discrete-time algorithm is provably convergent. The two stages therefore link a circuit-based description of a solution process to an implementable optimization method with a convergence guarantee.

The methodology recovers many classical optimization algorithms, including distributed ones, and supports exploring new algorithms. Recovering known methods shows that the circuit perspective can express established designs; the automated discretization then provides a route to extending that design space. The contribution is a reusable construction process for algorithms with convergence guarantees, rather than a single optimization update rule.
neurips-2024-optimization-algorithm-desi.tldr: The paper designs convex optimization algorithms by constructing convergent circuit dynamics and automatically converting them into provably convergent discrete updates.

paragraphs: Value alignment becomes a collective decision problem when different people want an agent to pursue different outcomes. This paper considers individuals with distinct reward functions and optimal policies within a shared Markov decision process. It formalizes the task of choosing a desirable policy for the group as policy aggregation, placing disagreement between individuals at the center of the problem.

The authors approach aggregation through social choice theory. Their key mathematical connection represents ordinal preferences using volumes of subsets of the state-action occupancy polytope. This geometric object describes possible patterns of state and action occupancy. Relating preferences to regions of that object makes social choice methods applicable to the space of policies.

Using this connection, the paper shows how approval voting, Borda count, the proportional veto core, and quantile fairness can be practically applied to policy aggregation. These provide several ways to construct collective decisions from differing preferences. The contribution supplies a shared framework for applying those methods to agent behavior, making the choice of aggregation rule an explicit part of alignment.
neurips-2024-policy-aggregation-bdb3f5dd.tldr: Policy aggregation connects social choice methods with the geometry of achievable agent behavior to combine individuals' differing preferences.

paragraphs: The paper studies reinforcement learning with an objective and a constraint that both extend over an infinite horizon. The agent seeks a large expected discounted reward while keeping its expected discounted cost above a specified threshold. This lower-bound requirement is part of the stated problem. Discounting determines how strongly future rewards and costs contribute to these totals.

The authors introduce Primal-Dual Accelerated Natural Policy Gradient, or PD-ANPG, using momentum-based acceleration. For general parameterized policies, they establish an epsilon global optimality gap and epsilon constraint violation with sample complexity of order (1−gamma)⁻⁷ epsilon⁻², up to logarithmic factors. Here gamma is the discount factor, and epsilon specifies the desired accuracy for both performance and constraint satisfaction.

The bound improves the previous state of the art by a factor of order (1−gamma)⁻¹ epsilon⁻². It also matches the theoretical lower bound in its dependence on inverse accuracy. This is a specific sample-efficiency result: the claimed optimality concerns the epsilon dependence, while the bound separately retains its stated dependence on the discount factor.
neurips-2024-sample-efficient-constraine.tldr: PD-ANPG improves sample-complexity guarantees for constrained reinforcement learning and matches the theoretical lower bound in accuracy dependence.

paragraphs: Audio deepfake detectors often lose effectiveness on synthesis attacks they have not encountered during training. Their decisions can also be difficult to explain. SLIM addresses both issues by examining the relationship between speaking style and linguistic content. The proposed signal is a mismatch between these aspects of speech that can help distinguish fabricated audio from real recordings.

The method first uses self-supervised pretraining on real speech alone to learn dependencies between style and language. It then combines these learned features with standard pretrained acoustic features, such as Wav2vec representations, to train a classifier on real and fake samples. The mismatch features thus complement the broader acoustic information available to the detector.

With feature encoders frozen, SLIM outperforms benchmark methods on out-of-domain datasets while remaining competitive on in-domain data. Its learned features also quantify how closely style and linguistic content match in a sample, providing a basis for explaining a decision. The findings support this explicit relationship as both a generalization signal and an interpretable component of the evaluated detector.
neurips-2024-slim-style-linguistics-mism.tldr: SLIM learns style-language dependencies in real speech to improve deepfake detection on unfamiliar data and help explain its decisions.

paragraphs: Online classification asks a learner to handle examples as they arrive, potentially under an adversary's influence. This paper studies a smoothed setting in which each example is drawn from a distribution with bounded density relative to a fixed base measure known to the learner. This restriction limits the adversary's choices while still allowing sequentially chosen distributions.

Earlier results established that smoothing makes online learning as easy as independent batch learning in the PAC framework for binary classification and scalar-valued regression. The authors show that this relationship need not extend to classification with an unbounded label space. They construct a hypothesis class that is PAC learnable from independent batch data but is not learnable in the smoothed online model.

This counterexample establishes that the size of the label space can matter to the relationship between the two learning settings. The paper also identifies a condition under which PAC learnability is sufficient for smoothed online learnability. The contribution therefore includes both a separation result and a positive condition that restores the implication.
neurips-2024-smoothed-online-classificat.tldr: With an unbounded label space, PAC batch learnability need not imply smoothed online learnability, although a sufficient condition can restore that implication.

paragraphs: Sparse-reward reinforcement learning is difficult because useful feedback may arrive only after a long, coordinated sequence of actions. Skills extracted from demonstrations can supply reusable behaviors, helping an agent work with meaningful sequences. However, existing skill-learning methods can make both extracting those skills and using them during policy inference expensive.

This paper introduces a demonstration-based skill extraction method inspired by Byte-Pair Encoding, a tokenization algorithm from natural language processing. It applies the idea of building useful sequence units to robot or agent behavior. The resulting skills form a finite set of interpretable behaviors, giving the policy a collection of reusable action patterns.

The authors report strong performance across a variety of tasks, alongside 1,000-fold faster skill extraction and 100-fold faster policy inference. They also show that skills extracted from 1% of the demonstrations in one task can transfer to a loosely related task. These findings support a simple sequence-based approach as an efficient way to obtain reusable skills in the evaluated sparse-reward settings.
neurips-2024-subwords-as-skills-tokeniza.tldr: A tokenization-inspired method extracts interpretable skills from demonstrations, reporting large speedups and transfer to a loosely related task.

paragraphs: Brain imaging can reveal anatomical connections and relationships between regional activity, but connecting these two views remains challenging. NeuroPath studies the coupling between structural connectivity and functional connectivity through graph representation learning. The aim is to give learned brain representations a neuroscience-informed structure that helps connect anatomy with observed functional relationships.

The central idea is a topological detour. A direct functional connection between two regions may be supported by a multi-hop pathway in the structural graph. Considering that functional link together with its structural detour forms a loop linking the two connectivity views. NeuroPath builds a multi-head self-attention mechanism around these pathways to learn representations from paired structural and functional graphs.

The resulting features can support downstream applications such as task recognition and disease diagnosis. Evaluations on Human Connectome Project and UK Biobank data include supervised and zero-shot learning settings, with reported state-of-the-art performance. These results indicate the potential of explicitly modeling structure-function coupling for connectome representation learning, while the proposed pathways remain putative descriptions of the underlying relationships.
neurips-2024-textit-neuropath-a-neural-p.tldr: NeuroPath links functional brain connections to multi-hop anatomical pathways to learn useful representations from paired connectivity graphs.

paragraphs: Graph homophily describes the tendency of connected nodes to share characteristics. Common measures focus on whether neighboring nodes have matching labels, yet these measures do not consistently track graph neural network performance. The paper argues that label agreement captures only part of the relevant similarity and separates homophily into label, structural, and feature components.

The proposed structural and feature measures account for neighborhood consistency and dependencies among node features. To study how all three components interact, the authors build a Contextual Stochastic Block Model in which the three homophily measures control graph topology and feature generation. Theoretical analysis of this model leads to Tri-Hom, a composite metric that combines the three aspects.

Synthetic experiments verify the theoretical conclusions and the effectiveness of Tri-Hom in the proposed model. On 31 real-world benchmark datasets, Tri-Hom has significantly higher correlations with model performance than 17 metrics focused on a single aspect. The findings support examining these forms of similarity together when relating graph properties to GNN performance.
neurips-2024-what-is-missing-for-graph-h.tldr: Tri-Hom combines label, structural, and feature homophily, showing stronger correlations with GNN performance than single-aspect metrics in the reported evaluation.

paragraphs: Embedding models convert objects into numerical representations that can support many downstream tasks. Comparing them usually requires task-specific experiments and sufficiently representative datasets. Those evaluations can be expensive or difficult to organize. This paper develops a common comparison framework intended to help identify promising embedding models before investing in extensive downstream testing.

The theoretical foundation uses sufficiency and informativeness to reason about the information represented by different embedders. From these concepts, the authors derive a tractable criterion called information sufficiency. This criterion supports a self-supervised ranking procedure that is independent of a particular downstream task, offering a shared basis for comparison across candidate models.

Experiments in natural language processing and molecular biology show that the resulting rankings align closely with embedding models' ability to support downstream tasks. This empirical alignment makes the method useful for prioritizing model trials. The stated result is a practical screening tool supported across these domains; it does not establish that the ranking must identify the best model for every possible task.
neurips-2024-when-is-an-embedding-model-.tldr: An information-sufficiency criterion ranks embedding models without a specific downstream task and empirically helps identify promising models to test.

paragraphs: Language models cache previous tokens' key and value states to avoid recomputing them, but long sequences make this cache large. Adaptive compression assigns more precision to important tokens. ZipCache addresses two difficulties with this approach: inaccurate importance estimates can damage performance, and the compression machinery itself can add memory use and generation latency.

The method introduces channel-separable tokenwise quantization to reduce the storage required for quantization parameters. It then uses normalized attention scores that account for the attention matrix's lower-triangular structure to identify salient tokens and assign their bit widths. An efficient approximation avoids dependence on full attention scores, allowing compatibility with fast attention implementations such as FlashAttention.

For Mistral-7B on GSM8k, the reported cache compression is 4.98-fold with a 0.38% accuracy drop. A separate LLaMA3-8B evaluation with input length 4096 reports reductions of 37.3% in prefill latency, 56.9% in decoding latency, and 19.8% in GPU memory use. These results show the benefits of combining selective precision with low-overhead compression in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2024-zipcache-accurate-and-effic.tldr: ZipCache combines low-overhead quantization with token-importance estimates to compress language-model caches while preserving accuracy and accelerating generation.
